The reproductive biology of the gray short-tailed opossum reveals several remarkable adaptations for a small marsupial. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 32.6 °C [T = 32.6 °C], the gestation period lasts approximately 15 days [tg = approximately 15 days], which is remarkably brief even by marsupial standards and reflects the accelerated developmental schedule characteristic of this species. Neonates emerge from the birth canal at a remarkably undeveloped state, each newborn weighing a mere 0.1 grams [Wwb = 0.1 grams] — a testament to the extremely altricial nature of marsupial birth. These minuscule newborns must immediately navigate from the urogenital opening to the teat, a journey that would be inconceivable for a eutherian mammal of similar developmental stage. The rapid gestational timeline and minimal investment in individual offspring at birth are hypothesized to represent an adaptation to fluctuating resource availability in their natural habitat.

Reproductive output in captive colonies of Monodelphis domestica has been quantified with considerable precision. Litter size typically consists of nine pups per litter [N_R_i = nine pups per litter], and females are capable of producing up to four litters per year [F_R_i = up to four litters per year] when maintained under optimal conditions, yielding a maximum reproduction rate of 36 pups per year [Ri = 36 pups per year]. This prolific reproductive schedule, facilitated by the shortened gestation period, allows a single female to generate substantial annual recruitment potential. The thermoneutral zone for these animals is centered around 32.6 °C [T = 32.6 °C], a temperature that optimizes metabolic efficiency and supports the high energetic demands of continuous breeding. Comparisons with other small didelphids suggest that this elevated reproductive tempo is somewhat unusual, though it aligns with the species' r-selected life-history strategy and its ability to colonize disturbed habitats where rapid population turnover confers a distinct advantage.

Developmental milestones in this species follow a carefully orchestrated sequence that is tightly coupled to maternal care. At approximately 53 days after birth [tx = approximately 53 days after birth], when maintained at 32.6 °C [T = 32.6 °C], the young undergo weaning and achieve nutritional independence from the mother. At this point, a typical juvenile weighs around 20.3 grams [Wwx = around 20.3 grams], having undergone an impressive mass gain from the initial neonatal weight. This weaning mass represents a critical threshold, as the young must now subsist entirely on solid food items, transitioning from exclusive milk dependence to active foraging. The timing of this transition is relatively early compared to eutherian mammals of similar adult body size, reflecting the abbreviated maternal investment period characteristic of many marsupials. The developmental trajectory from birth to weaning is thus compressed into less than two months, a pace that is coordinated with the species' short lifespan.

Sexual maturation in female gray short-tailed opossums occurs after a defined juvenile growth period. Puberty is attained at approximately 122 days after birth [tp = approximately 122 days after birth] under standard thermal conditions of 32.6 °C [T = 32.6 °C], at which point females become capable of conceiving their first litter. This timing from birth to reproductive maturity is relatively protracted compared to the brief gestation period, indicating that a substantial portion of the pre-reproductive lifespan is dedicated to somatic growth. Female ultimate body mass reaches about 100 grams [Wwi = about 100 grams], a figure that represents the asymptotic size for adult females in captivity. Males, in contrast, achieve a larger adult body size, with a typical ultimate wet weight of approximately 150 grams [Wwi = approximately 150 grams], reflecting a pronounced sexual size dimorphism. This size disparity is thought to be linked to intrasexual competition for access to receptive females.

Longevity records for Monodelphis domestica indicate a relatively short lifespan, consistent with its high reproductive output and rapid life history. Under captive conditions maintained at 32.6 °C [T = 32.6 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 5.1 years [am = approximately 5.1 years], a duration that is moderate for a marsupial of this body size. This lifespan is sufficient to accommodate multiple breeding seasons, given the species' capacity for early sexual maturation at approximately 122 days after birth [tp = approximately 122 days after birth] and its rapid litter production at a temperature of 32.6 °C [T = 32.6 °C]. The physiological constraint imposed by such a short reproductive window is offset by the high annual fecundity achieved through the combination of sizable litters and frequent breeding events. Field studies suggest that free-living individuals may experience substantially shorter lifespans due to predation and environmental stressors, though direct comparative data remain sparse. The species thus exemplifies a classic fast-paced life history, trading extended longevity for high early reproductive output.
